title: Lactaid and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Dairy Cocktails and Timing
excerpt: Can you take Lactaid and drink alcohol? Why lactase pills and alcohol don't interact, which drinks contain lactose, how to time your dose, and when gut trouble needs a doctor.
metaDescription: Can you take Lactaid while drinking? Why lactase and alcohol don't interact, which drinks have lactose, how to time your dose, and when to see a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, for most people it's fine to take Lactaid (a lactase enzyme pill) and drink alcohol. There is no known chemical interaction between the two. Lactase works inside your gut on one thing only, the milk sugar called lactose, and alcohol doesn't change how it does that job. The catch is that Lactaid only solves the lactose part of a creamy cocktail. It does nothing about the alcohol, the sugar, the fat, or the stomach irritation that drinking causes on its own. So if you take a Lactaid with your White Russian and still wake up with cramps and a loose stomach, the pill may have worked fine. The drink was simply doing something the pill can't touch.

**The quick rules:** Take Lactaid with the first sip of a dairy drink, not an hour before. If you keep drinking creamy drinks over a long evening, you'll likely need another dose, following the package directions. Beer, wine, and straight spirits generally contain no lactose, so you don't need a lactase pill for them. Milk stouts, cream liqueurs, eggnog, and anything made with milk or cream do contain lactose. And remember that alcohol can upset your stomach on its own, so gut trouble after drinking isn't always a lactose problem.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining Lactaid and alcohol if** you have a diagnosed digestive condition (such as celiac disease, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or IBS), you're not sure whether your symptoms are actually from lactose, you have diabetes or another condition that affects how you handle sugar, or you're pregnant. **See a doctor promptly if** you have severe or worsening belly pain, vomiting you can't stop, blood in your stool or black, tarry stool, a fever with diarrhea, or signs of dehydration such as dizziness when standing, very little urine, or confusion. If you have a true milk allergy (hives, swelling, wheezing, or trouble breathing after dairy), Lactaid will not protect you. Call 911 for any breathing trouble or throat swelling.

## How Lactaid Works, and Why Alcohol Doesn't Get in the Way

To understand why Lactaid and alcohol don't clash, it helps to know what each one actually does in your body.

**Lactose** is the natural sugar in milk. Your small intestine normally breaks it into two simpler sugars, glucose and galactose, using an enzyme called **lactase**. Those simple sugars then get absorbed into your blood. Many adults make less lactase than they did as children. This is very common worldwide and is especially common in people of East Asian, West African, Native American, and Middle Eastern descent. When there isn't enough lactase, undigested lactose moves on to the large intestine. There, gut bacteria ferment it, which produces gas, and the lactose also pulls water into the bowel. The result is the familiar set of symptoms: bloating, gas, cramps, rumbling, and sometimes diarrhea, usually starting thirty minutes to a few hours after eating dairy.

**Lactaid pills** (and store brands of lactase) contain the lactase enzyme itself, usually made from a type of fungus. When you swallow one alongside dairy, the enzyme mixes with the food in your stomach and small intestine and helps break down the lactose before it can reach the large intestine. It doesn't get absorbed into your body in any meaningful way. It simply works on the food in your gut and then gets digested itself, like any other protein.

**Alcohol**, on the other hand, is absorbed mainly through the stomach and small intestine into the bloodstream and is broken down mostly by the liver. It doesn't need lactase, and lactase doesn't touch it.

That's the core reason there's no meaningful interaction:

- Lactaid works locally in the gut on lactose. It isn't processed by the liver and doesn't affect the enzymes that break down alcohol.
- Alcohol doesn't destroy the enzyme in a single drink's worth of exposure in any way that's been shown to matter in practice.
- Neither one makes the other stronger, weaker, or more dangerous in the way that, say, alcohol and acetaminophen or alcohol and sedatives can.

Lactase products are sold in the US as dietary supplements, and their labels don't carry an alcohol warning. That fits with what's known about how they work. As always, the labels are the final word for the specific product you buy, so read yours.

### The part most articles skip: alcohol can mimic lactose intolerance

Here's where people get confused. Alcohol by itself can cause many of the same gut symptoms that lactose does:

- **It irritates the stomach lining**, which can cause nausea and a burning or crampy feeling.
- **It speeds up the movement of the gut** in many people, which leaves less time for water to be absorbed and leads to looser stools. This is one of the main reasons diarrhea after drinking is so common. Our guide to [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) explains this in more detail.
- **It changes the balance of gut bacteria**, especially with heavy or regular drinking.
- **Sugary mixers and syrups** can pull water into the gut and cause their own bloating and gas.

So if you're lactose intolerant and you have three mudslides, there are at least three things working against your stomach at once: the lactose, the alcohol, and the sugar and fat. Lactaid can take care of the first one. It can't do anything about the other two. That's why some people take a lactase pill, still feel rough, and decide the pill "doesn't work with alcohol." Usually the pill worked. The alcohol was just doing its own damage.

## Can You Take Lactaid While Drinking?

Yes. If you're having a drink that contains dairy, taking Lactaid at the same time is the right way to use it. Lactase only works while it's mixed in with the lactose, so the timing matters more than anything else.

**How to time it:**

1. **Take it with your first sip or bite.** Lactaid's own directions say to take it with the first bite of dairy food. For a drink, that means with your first sip, not an hour before you leave the house.
2. **Re-dose if the night goes on.** The enzyme doesn't hang around for hours. The package directions on standard Lactaid products tell you to take another dose if you keep eating dairy for a while after the first one (the label gives the specific window for that product). If you have a creamy cocktail at 8 p.m. and another at 10 p.m., you'll likely need a second dose with the second drink.
3. **Match the dose to the dairy.** A splash of cream in a coffee drink is a lot less lactose than a big eggnog or a milkshake-style cocktail. Some people need more than one pill for larger amounts. Follow the label on how many you can take at once and don't exceed it.

**What not to do:** Don't take extra Lactaid "just in case" before drinking beer, wine, or spirits that don't contain dairy. It won't do anything, because there's no lactose for it to work on, and it won't help with a hangover.

## Does Alcohol Contain Lactose?

Most alcoholic drinks contain no lactose at all. Lactose only comes from milk, so it's only in drinks that have milk, cream, whey, or added lactose. Here's how the common categories break down.

### Usually lactose-free

- **Beer (most styles).** Beer is brewed from grain, water, hops, and yeast. Standard lagers, ales, IPAs, and pilsners don't contain lactose.
- **Wine.** Red, white, rosé, and sparkling wines don't contain lactose. Some wines are processed with milk-derived fining agents (such as casein), but these are milk proteins, not lactose, and are mostly removed. This matters more for people with a milk allergy than for lactose intolerance.
- **Straight spirits.** Vodka, gin, rum, tequila, whiskey, and brandy are distilled, and distillation leaves milk sugar behind even if there were any to begin with. Plain spirits are lactose-free.
- **Hard seltzers and most ciders.** These are generally made without dairy.

### Contains lactose

- **Milk stouts and "pastry" or milkshake-style beers.** Brewers add lactose on purpose to these beers because yeast can't ferment it, so it leaves sweetness and a creamy body behind. If a beer is called a milk stout, sweet stout, cream stout, or milkshake IPA, assume it has lactose. Some brewers list it, and some don't.
- **Cream liqueurs.** Irish cream liqueurs (Baileys is the best-known), rum cream, tequila cream, and similar products are made with real dairy cream, so they contain lactose.
- **Eggnog** (whether store-bought or homemade with milk and cream).
- **Any cocktail with milk, cream, half-and-half, ice cream, or condensed milk.**

### Check the label

- **Flavored or "dessert" spirits and liqueurs.** Some contain dairy, many don't. If it looks creamy, check.
- **Ready-to-drink canned cocktails** that are creamy or "latte-style."
- **Some cocktail mixers.** Piña colada mix, for example, usually relies on coconut cream (which is dairy-free), but some brands add milk ingredients.

If you have a true milk allergy rather than lactose intolerance, the rules are stricter. You need to avoid milk proteins, not just lactose, so you should read labels carefully and ask about ingredients at bars. Lactaid won't help with an allergy at all.

## Dairy Cocktails: Which Ones Carry the Most Lactose?

The amount of lactose depends on how much milk or cream goes into the drink. You don't need exact numbers to get a sense of the risk. Milk generally has more lactose per cup than heavy cream does, because cream is mostly fat and the lactose is in the watery part of milk. Ice cream and sweetened condensed milk can be quite high. Roughly, from more to less:

- **Higher lactose:** boozy milkshakes, mudslides made with ice cream, eggnog, milk punch, a White Russian made with whole milk, and large creamy holiday drinks.
- **Moderate:** a White Russian made with cream, a Brandy Alexander, a Grasshopper, a Golden Cadillac, or a standard pour of Irish cream on ice.
- **Lower:** a splash of Irish cream in coffee, or a small cream float on an Irish coffee.

People with mild lactose intolerance can often handle a small amount of lactose without symptoms, especially alongside food. People with more severe intolerance may react to even a small pour. Your own experience is the best guide.

## Lactaid Milk and Alcohol: Lactose-Free Cocktails

Lactaid also makes lactose-free milk, and it's a good option if you want to make creamy drinks at home without needing a pill. Lactose-free milk is regular cow's milk with the lactase enzyme added during processing, so the lactose has already been broken down into glucose and galactose before you drink it. That's why it tastes a little sweeter than regular milk.

**It mixes just like regular milk.** You can swap it into a White Russian, a milk punch, an eggnog, or a boozy hot chocolate. A few tips:

- **Watch out for curdling.** Any milk can curdle when it meets acidic ingredients like citrus juice, or some liqueurs that are both acidic and strong. Lactose-free milk behaves the same way. Add the milk last and stir gently, or use cream, which holds up better.
- **Lactose-free cream and half-and-half** exist too and work well in drinks that call for cream.
- **The sweetness adds up.** Because lactose-free milk tastes sweeter, you may want to cut back on syrup or sweet liqueur in the recipe.
- **Plant milks are another route.** Oat, almond, soy, and coconut milk are naturally lactose-free. Oat milk tends to be the creamiest and closest to dairy in cocktails. These are also the safer choice if you have a milk allergy, since lactose-free cow's milk still contains milk proteins.

The alcohol in the drink is exactly the same no matter which milk you use. Lactose-free milk doesn't make a cocktail any less strong or any easier on your liver.

## Lactose Intolerance and Alcohol: Can Drinking Make It Worse?

This is a fair question, and the answer has two parts.

**In the short term,** drinking and dairy together can feel worse than dairy alone, even with Lactaid. As explained above, alcohol speeds up the gut and irritates it, so any lactose that slips past the enzyme may cause symptoms sooner and more strongly. Drinking on an empty stomach makes all of this worse. Eating a real meal before and during drinking slows alcohol absorption and gives your gut something to work with.

**In the long term,** heavy regular drinking can damage the lining of the small intestine, which is where lactase is made. Inflammation or damage to that lining can lower lactase levels for a while. Doctors call this kind of temporary loss "secondary" lactase deficiency, because it's caused by something else rather than by genetics. Other things can cause it too, such as a stomach bug, celiac disease, or inflammatory bowel disease. When the underlying cause settles down, lactase levels often recover.

For a social drinker who has a few drinks on a weekend, this isn't usually the main issue. But if you've noticed dairy bothers you more than it used to, and you've been drinking more often, it's a reasonable thing to mention to your doctor. It's also worth knowing that new dairy trouble can have other causes that are worth checking, which is why a doctor's visit makes more sense than guessing.

## Is It Lactose, or Is It the Alcohol? How to Tell

If your stomach is upset after a night of drinks, it can be hard to tell what caused it. Here's a rough way to sort it out.

**More likely lactose if:**

- Your symptoms are mainly gas, bloating, rumbling, and cramps, sometimes with loose stools.
- They show up within about thirty minutes to two hours after a dairy drink.
- You get the same symptoms from dairy when you're not drinking.
- They don't happen on nights when you drink only beer, wine, or spirits.

**More likely the alcohol if:**

- You get loose stools or cramps even on nights with no dairy at all.
- Your symptoms are more about nausea, a burning stomach, or heartburn.
- They show up the next morning along with other hangover symptoms like headache, thirst, and fatigue.
- They're worse after a lot of drinks, sugary mixers, or drinking without food.

**Probably both if** you had several creamy cocktails and your stomach is upset in every way at once. That's common and isn't a sign that something is wrong with you. Our guides to [gas after drinking](/never-hungover/gas-after-drinking) and [stomach pain after drinking](/never-hungover/stomach-pain-after-drinking) go deeper into the alcohol side of the picture.

A simple test: try the same dairy drink at home, sober, with food and a Lactaid, and see how you feel. Then try a non-dairy drink on a separate night. Comparing the two tells you a lot more than guessing after a mixed night out.

## Can You Combine Lactaid with Other Stomach Medicines and Alcohol?

People often reach for more than one product when their stomach is upset. Here's how Lactaid fits with the common ones.

- **Gas relief (simethicone, such as Gas-X).** Simethicone works in the gut to break up gas bubbles and isn't absorbed. It's commonly used alongside lactase. See our page on [Gas-X and alcohol](/never-hungover/gas-x-and-alcohol) for the alcohol side.
- **Pepto-Bismol (bismuth subsalicylate).** This one has a salicylate in it, which is related to aspirin, and that matters for people who drink heavily or have stomach bleeding risks. Our [Pepto-Bismol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/pepto-bismol-and-alcohol) covers the details.
- **Anti-diarrhea medicine (loperamide, such as Imodium).** It's sometimes used for occasional diarrhea, but it isn't meant for diarrhea with fever or blood, and you should follow the label carefully.
- **Probiotics.** Some people take them for general gut health. The evidence for specific benefits is mixed. Our [probiotics and alcohol](/never-hungover/probiotics-and-alcohol) page explains what's known.

Lactase itself isn't known to interact with these. The point to keep in mind is that each of these products has its own label and its own cautions, and adding alcohol on top can change things for some of them. If you take prescription medicines, especially for diabetes, your stomach, your bowels, or your mood, a quick check with a pharmacist is worth the five minutes. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) covers some of the broader alcohol and supplement questions.

## Does Dairy Help or Hurt a Hangover?

Some people swear by a glass of milk before going out to "line the stomach." There's no good evidence that milk prevents a hangover. A meal with protein, fat, and carbohydrate before drinking does slow how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, and milk is one source of those things. But it's not special, and for someone who's lactose intolerant, it can backfire by adding gut symptoms on top of the alcohol. If you want to use dairy this way, lactose-free milk or yogurt is the friendlier choice. Our page on [milk for a hangover](/never-hungover/milk-for-hangover) goes through the claims one by one.

The morning after, a heavy creamy breakfast can be rough on an already irritated stomach. If you're nauseous, simple, bland food and steady sips of water usually go down easier. If you do want dairy, the same rule applies: take your Lactaid with the first bite or choose lactose-free.

## When to See a Doctor

Most stomach upset from dairy and drinks passes within a day. But some signs mean you should get medical help rather than wait it out. This applies whether you think the cause is lactose, alcohol, or both.

> **See a doctor promptly, or go to urgent care, if you have:**
>
> - Severe belly pain, or pain that keeps getting worse
> - Vomiting that won't stop, or you can't keep water down
> - Blood in your vomit or stool, or black, tarry stool
> - Diarrhea with a fever, or diarrhea lasting more than two days
> - Signs of dehydration: dizziness when you stand up, a racing heart, very little or very dark urine, or confusion
>
> **Call 911 for:** trouble breathing, swelling of the lips, tongue, or throat, or hives spreading over the body after dairy. These are signs of an allergic reaction, not lactose intolerance, and Lactaid does nothing for them. Also call 911 if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, or has a seizure.
>
> **Book a regular appointment if:** you've recently started reacting to dairy when you didn't before, you have ongoing diarrhea or weight loss you can't explain, or you're relying on stomach medicines after most nights of drinking. These are worth looking into properly, and a doctor can check for things like celiac disease or bowel inflammation.

## Who Should Be More Careful

Lactaid is a very low-risk product for most people, and having one with a creamy cocktail is not a big deal. Still, a few groups should be more thoughtful.

- **People with diabetes.** Lactase splits lactose into glucose and galactose, which are absorbed more readily, and alcohol itself can push blood sugar down or up depending on the drink and whether you've eaten. Sugary creamy cocktails add a lot of sugar too. If you have diabetes, ask your doctor how to handle drinks with dairy and sugar.
- **People with galactosemia.** This is a rare inherited condition in which the body can't process galactose. Lactase products don't help, because they produce galactose. People with this condition need to avoid lactose entirely.
- **People with digestive conditions** such as IBS, Crohn's disease, ulcerative colitis, or celiac disease. Alcohol can trigger flares in some people, and gut symptoms can be harder to sort out. Your doctor or dietitian can help you work out what's safe.
- **People with a milk allergy.** As above, Lactaid won't protect you. Avoid dairy drinks entirely.
- **Pregnant people.** The issue isn't Lactaid. Health authorities advise avoiding alcohol during pregnancy.

## The Bottom Line on Drinking with Lactose Intolerance

If you're lactose intolerant and want to enjoy a creamy cocktail, the most effective plan is simple:

1. **Know which drinks have lactose.** Beer, wine, and straight spirits generally don't. Milk stouts, cream liqueurs, eggnog, and milk or cream cocktails do.
2. **Take Lactaid with your first sip,** and take another dose later if you keep drinking dairy drinks, following the label.
3. **Or skip the problem** by making drinks at home with lactose-free milk, lactose-free cream, or oat milk.
4. **Eat a real meal** before and while you drink.
5. **Pace yourself and alternate with water.** Fewer, slower drinks are easier on your stomach and everything else.
6. **Don't blame every upset stomach on lactose.** Alcohol and sugar cause plenty of gut trouble on their own.

For the alcohol side of the night, the habits with the best evidence are still the basics: drink less, drink slower, eat, and hydrate. Our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) walks through them.

Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a plant compound studied for its effects on how the body handles alcohol. Most of the research is in animals and in the lab, and human evidence is still limited, so it's best seen as an optional extra rather than a fix. It doesn't affect lactose or replace Lactaid, and there's no good evidence that it prevents hangovers on its own. If you want to try it, a straightforward, good-value option is [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically take it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol with Lactaid?**

Yes. There's no known interaction between lactase enzyme pills and alcohol. Lactaid works in your gut on lactose and isn't processed by the liver, so it doesn't affect how your body handles alcohol. Just remember it only helps with the lactose in a dairy drink, not with the stomach upset that alcohol can cause on its own.

**When should I take Lactaid before a dairy cocktail?**

Take it with your first sip, not long before. Lactase only works while it's mixed in with the lactose. If you have more dairy drinks over the next few hours, you'll likely need another dose. Follow the package directions for how often and how many you can take.

**Does beer or wine have lactose?**

Most beer and wine don't. The exceptions are milk stouts, sweet or cream stouts, and milkshake-style beers, which often have lactose added on purpose. Some wines are fined with milk proteins, but that's a concern for milk allergy rather than lactose intolerance. Straight spirits like vodka, gin, rum, tequila, and whiskey are lactose-free.

**Does Baileys have lactose?**

Yes. Irish cream liqueurs, including Baileys, are made with dairy cream, so they contain lactose. If you're lactose intolerant, take a lactase pill with your first sip or look for a dairy-free cream liqueur. If you have a milk allergy, avoid them.

**Can I use Lactaid milk in cocktails?**

Yes. Lactose-free milk works just like regular milk in drinks like White Russians, milk punch, and eggnog. It's a little sweeter, so you may want less syrup. Like any milk, it can curdle with acidic ingredients such as citrus, so add it last and stir gently.

**Why does my stomach still hurt after taking Lactaid and drinking?**

Probably because alcohol, sugar, and fat cause gut symptoms on their own. Alcohol irritates the stomach and speeds up the bowel, and sugary mixers can cause bloating. Lactaid can only break down lactose. If your stomach hurts even on nights without dairy, the alcohol is the more likely cause. See a doctor for severe or lasting pain, blood in your stool, or vomiting you can't stop.

**Can drinking alcohol cause lactose intolerance?**

Heavy, regular drinking can damage the lining of the small intestine, which is where lactase is made, and that can temporarily lower lactase levels. This is called secondary lactase deficiency, and it often improves once the cause settles down. If dairy has started bothering you when it didn't before, talk to your doctor, since other conditions can cause the same change.

**Does Lactaid help with a hangover?**

No. Lactaid only breaks down lactose. It has no effect on alcohol or on hangover symptoms like headache, fatigue, or thirst. It can stop lactose from adding to your stomach trouble if you're having dairy, but it won't make the alcohol easier on your body.
